title: Data explorer
Clade ages
text:
The table below provides crown and stem ages for fern orders, suborders, families, subfamilies, and genera, calculated directly from the current dated, consensus tree (FTOL v1.10.0). Because it is generated automatically from FTOL, these ages will update as the tree grows and dating estimates are refined with each new release.
Crown age is the age of the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of all species sampled in FTOL for a given taxon. Stem age is the age at which that taxon diverged from its sister lineage, i.e., the age of the node immediately ancestral to the crown node. Ages are in millions of years (Ma). The Order and Family columns show the higher classification of each taxon (Pteridophyte Phylogeny Group I 2016) and can be used to filter the table; only Polypodiales is formally divided into suborders, and not all families are divided into subfamilies.
Some taxa are not recovered as monophyletic in FTOL (see the Monophyletic column); for these, ages should be interpreted with caution, since the MRCA may also subtend species from other clades. Taxa represented by only a single sampled species have no meaningful crown age (shown as NA).










References

Pteridophyte Phylogeny Group I. 2016. “A Community-Derived Classification for Extant Lycophytes and Ferns.” Journal of Systematics and Evolution 54 (6): 563–603. https://doi.org/10.1111/jse.12229.

title: Contributing
text:
FTOL is a community-driven project. Contributions are welcome!
Please do let us know if something in the tree appears to need correction.
The best way to make a contribution is to file an issue on the FTOL github repo.

title: Downloads
text:
FTOL is available in several flavors:

The maximum likelihood (ML) tree has branchlengths in units of expected genetic change per site.
The consensus tree is the extended majority-rule consensus of the bootstrap trees, with units in expected genetic change per site.
The dated tree has branchlengths in units of time (Ma) and is ultrametric.
The backbone ML tree only includes species that have complete plastome sequences available.

All trees are rooted on algae (Zygnema) and include outgroup taxa, but Zygnema has been pruned from the dated trees. Node labels are bootstrap support values (%) measured with ultra-fast bootstrap (Hoang et al. 2018).
All trees are in Newick format.



The tree files are provided as part of a data archive (zip or tar.gz format).
Other files in the archive include DNA sequence alignments, GenBank accession numbers, and fossil calibration points.
All files are described in the README.txt file contained within the archive.

title: Tree Viewer
text:
The interactive tree visualization below shows higher taxonomic groups (genus, family, order, etc.) by color on the dated, consensus tree (outgroup not shown). Default coloring is by family. Species names will appear when zoomed in or hovering over a tip. The same visualization is available at Taxonium, where you can also upload other trees for viewing. For more details about using Taxonium, see the documentation.
If you want to view the tree in a desktop app, we recommend either Dendroscope3 or the Taxonium desktop app.

title: Methods
text:
For a full description of methods, see Nitta et al. (2022).
The goal of this project is to produce a maximally sampled global fern phylogeny.
All DNA sequence data were downloaded from GenBank. The current FTOL (v1.10.0) includes sequences up to 2026-10-04 (GenBank release 274).
Input data, including a database containing fern sequences from GenBank release 274, are available on FigShare.
Two datasets were produced:

The “plastome” dataset includes 79 loci obtained from whole plastomes for 1172 species (including outgroup taxa).
The “Sanger” dataset includes 7 plastid loci for 6,411 species (including outgroup taxa).

Phylogenetic analysis was carried out using maximum likelihood in IQ-TREE (Nguyen et al. 2015) in two steps. First, a backbone phylogeny was built using the plastome dataset. Next, the full phylogeny was built using the Sanger dataset with the backbone phylogeny as a constraint tree. For both analyses, all loci were concatenated and no partitioning was used.
The tree was dated using treePL (Smith and O’Meara 2012) with a set of 54 fossil constraints (not including the root).




References

Nguyen, Lam-Tung, Heiko A. Schmidt, Arndt von Haeseler, and Bui Quang Minh. 2015. “IQ-TREE: A Fast and Effective Stochastic Algorithm for Estimating Maximum-Likelihood Phylogenies.” Molecular Biology and Evolution 32 (1): 268–74. https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msu300.


Nitta, Joel H., Eric Schuettpelz, Santiago Ramírez-Barahona, and Wataru Iwasaki. 2022. “An Open and Continuously Updated Fern Tree of Life.” Frontiers in Plant Sciences 13. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2022.909768.


Smith, Stephen A, and Brian C. O’Meara. 2012. “treePL: Divergence Time Estimation Using Penalized Likelihood for Large Phylogenies.” Bioinformatics 28 (20): 2689–90. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bts492.

title: Fern Tree of Life
text:
A webportal hosting the Fern Tree of Life (FTOL) and associated data

FTOL is a global phylogeny of extant fern species based on plastid DNA sequences.
For a complete description, see Nitta et al. (2022).
FTOL is an on-going project and will be regularly updated as new sequence data become available.




References

Nitta, Joel H., Eric Schuettpelz, Santiago Ramírez-Barahona, and Wataru Iwasaki. 2022. “An Open and Continuously Updated Fern Tree of Life.” Frontiers in Plant Sciences 13. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2022.909768.
